source.title: Testing the Robustness of a BiLSTM-based Structural Story Classifier
source.authors: Aftab Hussain; Sai Durga Prasad Nanduri; Sneha Seenuvasavarathan

page_placements.theme: Consistent binary inversion differs from random labeling

record.file_problem: Text includes the full paper, though some experimental results are presented only in figures.
record.tranche_reason: Tests label-noise effects on a BiLSTM-based fake-news classifier in a new task and model setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for training loss and test accuracy under label flips. It does not report training error or whether the model reaches zero training error. Cited results from Arpit et al. are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study tests V4's test-performance component in a BiLSTM news classifier under increasing label-flip rates. It does not establish perfect training-set fitting. Binary label flipping also differs from independent random relabeling: 100% flips invert all labels, while 50% flips most closely approximate random labels.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors report that moderate noise sometimes improves test accuracy, speculate that structural learning rather than memorization explains this, and note reduced accuracy at high noise levels. That mechanism remains speculative; they call for further investigation and acknowledge the 134-example test set.
record.recipe_differences: The study flips a chosen fraction of binary news labels and evaluates a BiLSTM-based fake-news classifier; it does not use the original image-classification random-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise level and training stage; test accuracy fluctuates more across stages for noise-induced datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Training loss stays around 0.7 with 25% and 50% flips; the 100%-flipped condition improves during training and has lower loss than the other noisy conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-entropy training loss varies nonmonotonically with binary label-flip rate over a fixed training budget; this measure alone does not establish whether training classification error reaches zero.

record.problems: Test set was relatively small (134 samples), as the authors note. Training-loss and test-accuracy results are presented in figures without stated numeric values or uncertainty estimates. No training error is reported.
record.rows_left_out: No rows extracted: the relevant training-loss and test-accuracy findings are only described through figures and lack usable per-condition numeric values; the text does not establish training error or perfect fitting.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training error on completely random labels and chance-level test performance.
Time required to fit true versus random labels and convergence time as corruption increases; all conditions receive a fixed training budget.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian inputs.
Perfect training-set fitting, memorization of corrupted examples, and a demonstrated approach to chance under independent random relabeling.
Comparisons with and without explicit regularization; dropout is fixed at zero.
Separate learning trajectories for true-label patterns and corrupted examples.

missing.what: Qualitative V4 results need rows even without exact figure values: moderate-noise checkpoints outperform the clean baseline, while 75% and 100% flips reportedly reduce test accuracy. The record declares these outcomes omitted, but their text descriptions can support qualitative rows.

record.verdict_notes: No numerical test accuracies, chance comparison, training classification errors, or uncertainty estimates are supplied in the text. The authors' description of significant accuracy reductions is not accompanied by a reported statistical test. Fully inverted binary labels retain the original label structure, so the 100%-flip condition cannot stand for completely random labeling.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling, training error, and whether the original architecture and hyperparameters fit such labels.
Training time to fit true versus random labels and convergence as corruption increases.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
The paper studies label flips at 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%, but does not report training error or establish perfect fitting. Results are figure-only, with no usable per-condition values.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on fitting random labels and true-label generalization.
Whether true-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

relationships.condition: Moderate label-flip rates at selected training checkpoints
relationships.reason: Based on Section 5.2, with no extracted rows: 50% flips outperform the clean baseline at steps 120, 180, and 200, and 25% flips do so at step 160. Thus test error does not consistently increase with corruption in this setting.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy exceeded the clean baseline with 50% flips at steps 120, 180, and 200, and 25% flips at step 160.

source_check.reason: Section 5.2 explicitly reports higher test accuracy than the clean baseline with 50% flips at steps 120, 180, and 200 and 25% flips at step 160. For this condition group, V4's predicted test-performance degradation reverses.

relation.reason: The study directly measures training loss and test accuracy under increasing binary label-flip rates.

tranche.reason: Sections 5.2 and 6 explicitly report that increasing label noise need not decrease test accuracy, requiring qualification of V4's steadily worsening test-performance component.

source_check.notes: Perfect training-set fitting is not established; 100% binary flipping inverts every label rather than independently randomizing labels. The test set contains 134 samples. Section 5.1 explicitly supplies the approximate training-loss value 0.7 despite the pack's claim that numeric outcomes are unrecoverable.
